\section{Classifier settings}\label{sec:s_classifiers}
All classifiers are trained on original windows, standardised per channel with the statistics of the training fold, and evaluated on the original and on every reconstruction of the same held-out windows. KNN ($k=5$), an RBF SVM ($C=1$, Platt probabilities, one-vs-rest for the multilabel PTB-XL) and a random forest (300 trees) take the flattened window. The LSTM and GRU (64 and 32 units, dropout $0.2$) and a one-dimensional CNN (convolutions of 32 and 64 filters of width 5, max pooling, global average pooling and a 64-unit dense layer) take the $(T,C)$ window and are trained with Adam, batch size 64 and at most 20 epochs, with early stopping (patience 4) on the last 10\% of the training fold. Metrics are computed per fold and averaged over the three folds; the equivalence intervals resample the groups of the split (subjects, patients, events, stations or recordings).

\section{Recurrence-rate sensitivity of Hirata's reconstruction}\label{sec:s_hirata}
Table~\ref{tab:s_hirata} gives the 8-bit NMAE of Hirata's reconstruction against the recurrence rate used to threshold the image ($T=128$, 100 windows per dataset, every channel). The rate of $0.75$ used in the main text was fixed in advance; choosing the best rate per dataset with knowledge of the result lowers the error by at most \hirataGainUns{} on the unsigned and \hirataGainSig{} on the signed RP.

\section{Sampling rate at a fixed length and at a fixed duration}\label{sec:s_sampling}
Table~\ref{tab:s_sampling} separates the sampling rate from the window duration on PTB-XL. With 128 samples, a higher rate also means a shorter window; with a fixed duration of 1.28\,s, the number of samples grows with the rate. In both settings the conditioning $\sigma_2/\sigma_1$ falls and the error of the signed RP rises with the rate, while GASF, GADF and XIRP do not follow that trend. The ``native'' rows use the 100\,Hz files distributed with the dataset instead of resampling the 500\,Hz records.

\section{Sipers et al.\ and the geometric decoder on the same image}\label{sec:s_sipers}
The reconstruction of Sipers et al.\ assumes a periodic signal and a circular delay embedding, so in the main benchmark it decodes the circular variant of the RP, with the wrap state $(x_T,x_1)$ added, while the geometric decoder decodes the benchmark's non-circular RP. Table~\ref{tab:s_sipers} removes that difference: both decoders receive the identical circular image ($T=128$, 100 windows per dataset, every channel, 8-bit), the same pixel matrix and the same per-channel calibration, and on the signed RP both choose the reflection from the image alone with the same criterion, so any gap is due to the decoder. The circular RP is built on the states $(x_i,x_{i+1})$, $i=1,\ldots,T$, with $x_{T+1}=x_1$: it is the benchmark RP with one added state, the wrap state $(x_T,x_1)$, and the same 8-bit maps.

Sipers' method represents the window by its periodic extension, which a finite sequence always admits, so its hypotheses hold for the circular embedding of any window; the cost is the wrap state, which joins the last sample to the first and is not part of the recorded dynamics. With a node threshold of zero, the implementation is exact in floating point (median error $0$; maximum \sipZeroMaxClean{} on WISDM, Swarm and STEAD, and \sipZeroMaxPtb{} for the worst of \sipZeroPtbSeries{} PTB-XL series, where near-zero Fourier coefficients enter the division of Eq.~(15) of Sipers et al.); the error of the threshold used in the main text is therefore truncation, not a property of the method. The node threshold is a share of the largest Fourier power estimated from the image; it does not use the original series. It was chosen as the value that minimises Sipers' own 8-bit error in this sweep, which favours the method in the comparison. With the threshold of $0.01$ used by its authors, the error is \sipPaperTolMin{} to \sipPaperTolMax{} even in floating point, because our windows are broadband. The last columns sweep the node threshold of the Sipers decoder, the share of the largest Fourier power below which a frequency is discarded; Sipers et al.\ used $0.01$ without optimising it, and the main text uses $10^{-4}$, the best value at 8 bits in this sweep.
